theory.title: Theory
theory.hint: A neck-first syllabus — live examples on the fretboard below
theory.intro: Pick a topic, read the short lesson, and watch the fretboard below update. Use the buttons to switch examples — Drills links still open the practice tab.

pitchAndOctave.title: Pitch, pitch class & octave
pitchAndOctave.blurb: Why every note name returns after twelve frets.

p: Pitch is the exact highness or lowness of a sound. A pitch class groups every octave of the same note name together, so all C notes belong to pitch class C even though they sound at different heights.
Lead sheets usually care about pitch class: Cmaj7 tells you which note classes make the chord, not which octave or voicing to use.
Western equal temperament divides the octave into twelve semitones. Moving twelve frets up one string doubles the frequency and returns to the same pitch class.
That repeat is the fretboard's main landmark. Learn one twelve-fret region well, then recognize its shapes again an octave higher.
Turn on note names and follow one pitch class across all six strings. Its positions look irregular across strings, but every position repeats twelve frets later.
Then switch to degrees: the same physical markers now show each note's job relative to the selected root rather than its absolute name.

intervals.title: Intervals & degrees
intervals.blurb: Measure distance from a root with scale degrees and interval qualities.

p: A degree names a note's position relative to a tonal center: 1, 2, b3, 4, and so on. An interval names both its numbered span and quality: P1, M2, m3, P4.
Degrees are quick harmonic shorthand; qualities preserve the exact spelling and size. A b3 degree above C is Eb, and the interval C–Eb is a minor third. Tap a figure to place the dyad on the board.
Unisons, fourths, fifths, and octaves use perfect, diminished, or augmented quality. Seconds, thirds, sixths, and sevenths use major, minor, diminished, or augmented quality.
Count letter names for the number, then semitones for the quality. C–F# is an augmented fourth; C–Gb is a diminished fifth even though both sound at the same fret.
Intervals within one octave are simple. Carry a 2nd, 4th, or 6th above the octave and it becomes a compound 9th, 11th, or 13th.
On guitar, compare Degrees and Intervals on the same scale. The first reveals function; the second makes chord formulas and ear-training distances explicit.

spellingAndEnharmonics.title: Spelling & enharmonics
spellingAndEnharmonics.blurb: Choose note names that reveal the scale and harmony.

p: Enharmonic notes sound the same in equal temperament but are written differently: F# and Gb share a pitch, as do C# and Db. The spelling tells you how the note behaves.
A chord third must be some kind of third by letter. D–F# is a major third; writing D–Gb hides that structure behind the sound of a diminished fourth.
A seven-note scale normally uses each letter name once. F# major is F#–G#–A#–B–C#–D#–E#: E#, not F, is its leading tone.
That spelling makes the degrees readable and keeps stacked thirds visible. It also explains why key context can favor a sharp or flat name.

body.h: Fit the display to the scale
p: Fit Scale chooses names from the selected scale instead of forcing every black-key pitch into a global sharp or flat preference.
Compare Fit Scale with Flats while changing keys. Use the fixed choice when communicating a broad preference; use fitted spelling when studying actual scale grammar.

building.title: Building triads & seventh chords
building.blurb: Stack thirds, read formulas, and hear how one changed tone reshapes a chord.

p: A triad stacks two thirds above a root. Major is 1–3–5, minor is 1–♭3–5, diminished is 1–♭3–♭5, and augmented is 1–3–♯5.
Compare the formula strip, the staff stack, and the neck diagram. Tap any of them to load that triad on the board below.
Another stacked third creates a seventh chord. Major seventh is 1–3–5–7, dominant seventh is 1–3–5–♭7, and minor seventh is 1–♭3–5–♭7.
Half-diminished, written m7♭5, is 1–♭3–♭5–♭7. Fully diminished seventh lowers the last tone again to ♭♭7, producing an even stack of minor thirds.
Place chord tones and read their roles before worrying about fingering. A voicing may omit the fifth, double a tone, or spread notes across octaves without changing the core symbol.
Move only one marker at a time between examples. Hearing 3 become ♭3 or 7 become ♭7 turns a memorized formula into a practical sound.

inversionsAndSlash.title: Inversions & slash chords
inversionsAndSlash.blurb: Separate the harmonic root from the note in the bass.

p: The root gives a chord its identity; the bass is simply its lowest sounding note. Root position puts the root in the bass, while an inversion places another chord tone below it.
For Cmaj7, compare root position with E in the bass (first inversion). Tap either diagram to mirror it on the live board.
A slash chord writes chord/bass: C/E means a C chord with E as the lowest note. The bass may be a chord tone, an inversion, or a non-chord pedal or passing tone.
Read the symbol from left to right: establish the chord quality first, then satisfy the requested bass note.
A compact guitar voicing can support several names. If the Analyzer follows the bass but the musical context points elsewhere, pin the intended root and compare the alternate reading.
Practice moving only the bass under fixed upper voices. Smooth slash-chord motion often matters more than keeping every chord in root position.

extensionsAndAlts.title: Extensions & alterations
extensionsAndAlts.blurb: Add 9ths, 11ths, and 13ths without losing the chord underneath.

p: Continue stacking thirds above a seventh chord to reach the 9th, 11th, and 13th. They are compound versions of 2, 4, and 6, but the higher number implies a richer chord stack.
A Cmaj9 is built from 1–3–5–7–9; C9 uses 1–3–5–b7–9. The seventh distinguishes an extended dominant symbol from an added-note chord. Tap a diagram to load it below.
Guitar voicings rarely contain every theoretical tone. The root, 3rd, 7th, and selected color tones usually carry more information than the 5th.
The natural 11 can clash with a major 3rd, so major-family voicings often omit it or sharpen it to #11. The 13 may replace the 5th in a lean voicing.
Alterations such as b9, #9, #11, b5, #5, and b13 intensify a dominant chord's pull. They modify named tensions; they do not replace the underlying 3 and b7 that define dominant function.
In Chord Analyzer, click an alteration hook to open a scale featuring that color. Compare Lydian Dominant over 7#11 and the Altered scale over 7alt.

chords.title: Reading chord symbols
chords.blurb: Parse the lead-sheet stack from root through slash bass.

p: Read a lead-sheet symbol as root + quality + extension + alterations + /bass. In C#m9/G#, C# is the root, m is minor quality, 9 is the extension, and G# is the bass.
A bare letter means a major triad. C7 means dominant seventh, not major seventh; Cmaj7 explicitly names the major 7.
Symbols such as m, dim, aug, sus2, and sus4 alter the basic triad. Extension figures then add or imply upper chord tones.
Parentheses collect optional colors or alterations: G7(b9,#11). The symbol describes harmonic content, not a mandatory fretboard shape or doubling.
Start with the guide tones—the 3rd and 7th—then add the bass and one requested color. This produces a clear guitar part without trying to grip every implied tone.
Use alternate Analyzer readings as context checks. The best symbol is the one that explains the bass, function, and surrounding progression with the least strain.

harmony.title: Diatonic chords & ii–V–I
harmony.blurb: Stack the scale into chords, then hear its strongest common cadence.

p: Stack alternating scale tones above each degree to produce the diatonic chord set. In C major the seventh chords are Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7, and Bm7b5.
Roman numerals preserve each chord's scale position when the key changes. Uppercase suggests major, lowercase minor, and the quality marks complete diminished-family symbols.
Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 is ii–V–I in C: preparation, dominant tension, and arrival. The roots move by fifth, while the guide tones move efficiently by half or whole step.
The same pattern works in every major key. Learn the function and voice leading, then move the geometry rather than memorizing twelve unrelated progressions.
Open Ionian to inspect its scale chords, then send ii, V, and I to Chord Analyzer. Compare each chord's tones against the full scale on the neck.
Use Drills to build the cadence without labels. The exercise closes the loop from recognizing a formula to finding its notes under your fingers.

functionalHarmony.title: Functional harmony
functionalHarmony.blurb: Hear chords as tonic, predominant, or dominant motion.

p: Tonic function feels settled, predominant function moves away from tonic, and dominant function creates pressure to return. The common flow is T–PD–D–T.
In major, I is the clearest tonic, ii and IV are common predominants, and V or vii° supply dominant pull.
A chord's scale degree suggests a role, but meter, bass, duration, and neighboring chords shape what you hear. vi can prolong tonic or begin a deceptive turn.
Function describes directed motion rather than chord quality alone. A major chord can be tonic in one key, predominant in another, and dominant when temporarily tonicizing a new target.
In G7–Cmaj7, B rises to C and F falls to E. Those half-step resolutions make dominant-to-tonic motion clear even in a two-note guitar shell.
Compare I–IV–V–I with I–ii–V–I. The surface voicings differ, but both trace the same functional departure and return.

cadencesAndTurnarounds.title: Cadences & turnarounds
cadencesAndTurnarounds.blurb: Shape endings, detours, and returns with familiar harmonic routes.

p: An authentic cadence moves V–I and gives the strongest tonal close, especially when both chords and melody emphasize the tonic. A plagal cadence moves IV–I for a softer release.
A deceptive cadence redirects V to vi instead of I. The expected leading-tone resolution can remain while the bass avoids the tonic, extending the phrase.
A turnaround occupies the end of a phrase and points back to its beginning. I–vi–ii–V is a classic loop because each chord leads naturally toward the next.
Jazz turnarounds often add secondary dominants or substitutions, but their job remains practical: create momentum into the next tonic.
On guitar, keep one common tone where possible and move the other voices by the smallest interval. Cadential force survives even when roots are supplied by a bassist.
Loop each route and listen to expectation: closure for V–I, warmth for IV–I, surprise for V–vi, and renewed motion for the turnaround.

secondaryDominants.title: Secondary dominants
secondaryDominants.blurb: Borrow a dominant to spotlight a diatonic chord.

p: A secondary dominant is the V of a chord other than the home tonic. In C major, D7 is V/V because D7 is the dominant of G, the key's V chord.
Its F# lies outside C major and acts as a temporary leading tone to G. That chromatic note creates direction without requiring a full modulation.
V/V is read "five of five." This functional slash is not a bass slash: D7/F# names a voicing, while V/V names harmonic purpose.
Other common examples are V/ii leading to ii and V/vi leading to vi. The target usually arrives immediately or after a brief embellishment.
Play D7–G7–Cmaj7. The first dominant points to the second, and the second resolves home, creating a chain of descending fifths.
Track each chord's 3rd and b7 in Analyzer. Those guide tones reveal why the chromatic chord sounds directed rather than randomly outside the key.

minorHarmony.title: Harmony in minor keys
minorHarmony.blurb: Use natural, harmonic, and melodic minor as complementary resources.

p: Natural minor, or Aeolian, supplies the basic minor-key collection: 1–2–b3–4–5–b6–b7. In A minor its diatonic v chord is Em or Em7.
That minor v has weak dominant pull because it lacks the leading tone G#. Minor-key practice therefore often alters the seventh degree.
Harmonic minor raises b7 to 7, turning Em into E or E7 and creating a strong V–i resolution. The scale's b6-to-7 augmented second is a consequence of that harmonic need.
The resulting chord set mixes familiar and distinctive colors, including augmented III and fully diminished vii°7.
Melodic minor also raises b6 to 6, smoothing melodic motion while preserving the leading tone. Jazz practice commonly uses this form in both directions and mines its modes for chord-scale colors.
Treat the three scales as views of one minor-key system, not competing definitions. Choose tones according to melody, voice leading, and the chord currently sounding.

voiceLeading.title: Voice leading & guide tones
voiceLeading.blurb: Read the inner motion before reaching for full guitar shapes.

p: Voice leading treats each chord tone as part of a melodic line. Good motion often keeps common tones and moves remaining voices by step instead of making every hand shape jump.
The smoothest path is not always the nearest root-position chord. Inversions let the bass and upper voices travel independently.
The 3rd and 7th are guide tones because they define quality and function. In G7, B and F form a tritone that resolves inward to C and E in Cmaj7.
A two-note shell can therefore state V–I more clearly than a dense voicing whose important tones are buried. Tap G7, then Cmaj7, and watch the roles.
Place V and I in Analyzer, identify every role, then choose nearby copies of the guide tones on adjacent strings. Add roots or colors only after the motion is audible.
Practice in several string sets. Reading roles first prevents a familiar grip from hiding doubled notes, omitted tones, or awkward melodic leaps.

modes.title: The church modes
modes.blurb: Seven major-scale rotations, each with its own center and characteristic color.

p: Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, and Locrian can be generated from rotations of one major scale. C Ionian and D Dorian share notes, but they do not share a tonic.
A mode becomes audible when harmony, phrasing, and emphasis establish its own root. Merely starting a C-major run on D does not guarantee a Dorian sound.
Compare each mode with a familiar major or minor baseline. Lydian is major with #4, Mixolydian is major with b7, Dorian is minor with 6, and Phrygian is minor with b2.
Aeolian's b6 supports natural-minor gravity; Locrian's b5 makes its tonic triad diminished and unstable. Ionian is the unaltered major reference.
Drone the modal tonic or loop a simple tonic chord, then target the characteristic note and resolve it deliberately. This separates modal color from parent-scale fingering.
Keep the root fixed while switching modes in Explore. The changed markers show the exact intervals responsible for each new sound.

melodicMinor.title: Melodic minor & its modes
melodicMinor.blurb: A minor tonic with natural 6 and 7, plus essential modern dominant colors.

p: Jazz melodic minor is 1–2–b3–4–5–6–7 in both directions. It combines a minor 3rd with major 6th and 7th for a tense but lyrical minor color.
Over a minor-major seventh chord, the scale states every essential tone and offers natural 9, 11, and 13.
The fourth mode is Lydian Dominant: 1–2–3–#4–5–6–b7. Its 3 and b7 fit a dominant chord while #4 supplies the #11 color.
Use it over 7#11, especially when a plain Mixolydian 4 would rub against the major 3rd.
The seventh mode is Super Locrian, commonly called the Altered scale. Relative to its root it contains b9, #9, b5 or #11, and b13 around a dominant shell.
Use it over 7alt, then resolve altered tensions by half step into the target chord. The destination makes the outside color intelligible.

harmonicMinor.title: Harmonic minor & Phrygian Dominant
harmonicMinor.blurb: Strengthen minor-key dominant motion and explore its b2–3 color.

p: Harmonic minor is 1–2–b3–4–5–b6–7. Raising the natural-minor b7 creates a leading tone and turns the v chord into a major V or V7.
The augmented second between b6 and 7 is the scale's unmistakable melodic gap. It can sound dramatic, classical, metal, or regionally inflected depending on phrasing.
The fifth mode is Phrygian Dominant: 1–b2–3–4–5–b6–b7. Its major 3rd and b7 outline a dominant chord, while b2 and b6 supply its characteristic tension.
In A harmonic minor, E Phrygian Dominant fits E7 and points back to Am. The mode is a dominant view of the same minor-key material.
Hold an E or E7 drone, emphasize F and G#, then resolve into A minor. The half-step F–E and G#–A motions reveal both the modal color and its function.
Map A harmonic minor first, then switch the root to E without changing the pitch collection. Listen for the center to move from minor tonic to dominant.

pentatonicAndBlues.title: Pentatonic & blues scales
pentatonicAndBlues.blurb: Five sturdy notes, then one blue note that changes the phrasing.

p: Major pentatonic is 1–2–3–5–6. It removes the major scale's two semitone pairs, leaving an open collection that fits many folk, country, pop, and soul melodies.
Minor pentatonic is 1–b3–4–5–b7. Relative major and minor pentatonics share notes, but phrasing and harmonic center decide which sound you hear.
The common minor blues scale adds b5 between 4 and 5. That passing tone is expressive because it rubs against stable chord tones and wants motion.
Do not treat every scale tone equally. Bend toward chord tones, linger on b3 or b7 where the harmony supports them, and use b5 as tension rather than a parking place.
Guitar box patterns are useful navigation, but target notes make a solo follow the progression. Mark each chord's root, 3rd, and 7th inside the pentatonic map.
Compare major and minor pentatonic over the same blues tonic. Their overlap supports familiar call-and-response, while their different thirds create the expressive major/minor blend.

symmetricScales.title: Symmetric scales
symmetricScales.blurb: Repeat interval patterns to create ambiguous, reusable tension.

p: The whole-tone scale uses six consecutive whole steps. With no semitones, perfect fifths, or unique internal hierarchy, it sounds floating and resistant to a single tonal center.
Its 1–3–#5 outline fits augmented chords, while 9, #11, and b13 can color dominant harmony.
The diminished scale alternates whole and half steps across eight notes. Whole–half supports diminished-seventh harmony; half–whole is commonly placed over dominant b9 chords.
Because the pattern repeats every minor third, one diminished collection serves several roots and dominant chords. That symmetry is powerful but can obscure direction.
Sequence a small fingering in minor thirds to hear the geometry, then break the pattern by resolving a voice a half step into the next chord.
Use the neck view to compare whole–half and half–whole from the same root. Their notes overlap, but where the half step begins changes the chord they describe.

bebopAndChromatic.title: Bebop scales & chromatic motion
bebopAndChromatic.blurb: Use passing tones to place chord tones on strong beats.

p: A bebop scale adds a chromatic passing tone to a seven-note scale. In an even stream of eighth notes, the extra note can place stable chord tones consistently on downbeats.
The passing tone is a rhythmic and melodic device, not a new tonic. Its success depends on where the line begins, where it lands, and which chord is sounding.
Bebop dominant adds a major 7 passing tone to Mixolydian: 1–2–3–4–5–6–b7–7. Over a dominant chord, 1, 3, 5, and b7 can line up on strong beats.
Bebop major adds #5 or b6 to the major scale. The added tone bridges 5 and 6 while preserving the major chord as the line's structural target.
Approach a chord tone from a half step above, below, or both. Enclosures make a line sound connected to the harmony even when several notes lie outside the parent scale.
Practice one octave with a metronome and vary the starting degree. If chord tones drift onto weak beats, change the pickup or direction rather than blaming the scale.

systems.title: CAGED, NPS & Berklee positions
systems.blurb: Organize one neck-wide scale into different practice maps.

p: CAGED connects five movable regions named for open C, A, G, E, and D chord forms. Each region links chord tones, arpeggios, and surrounding scale notes.
The names describe visual ancestry, not the current key. In any key, the five regions repeat in order and overlap along the neck.
NPS organizes ascending scale tones with a fixed count—usually three or four—on each string. It favors repeated picking and legato mechanics and exposes diagonal neck movement.
The fingering is regular in note count, not fret span. Position shifts and the tuning break between G and B still require attention.
Berklee-style seven-position practice places one compact window on each scale degree. The forms keep the whole scale available while limiting the hand to a readable area.
No system owns the correct notes. Compare all three over one root, name degrees inside every form, and use the map that serves the phrase or technique you are practicing.

quartalHarmony.title: Quartal harmony
quartalHarmony.blurb: Stack fourths for open, modal voicings that resist ordinary triad labels.

p: Tertian harmony stacks thirds to produce triads and seventh chords. Quartal harmony stacks fourths, creating wider structures such as C–F–Bb.
Perfect fourths dominate the sound, but a scale-constrained stack may include an augmented or diminished fourth. Those changes connect the voicing to its mode.
A quartal voicing can support several roots because it may not contain a conventional 3rd. Context, bass, melody, and neighboring shapes determine its function.
This ambiguity makes fourth stacks useful for modal comping, suspended textures, and parallel movement where a fixed chord symbol is less important than color.
Open the Quartal layer, choose a string set and height, and follow the connected scale tones. Shift the stack through the mode while listening for stable and tense degrees.
Add a separate bass note to test possible roots. The same upper structure can become a sus chord, an extended dominant color, or a rootless minor voicing.

readingTheNeck.title: Reading the neck
readingTheNeck.blurb: Combine Display, Analyzer, and Drills into one learning loop.

body.h: See one layer at a time
p: Use Display intentionally: Names answer where notes are, Degrees show scale function, and Intervals expose exact distance from the root. Switch views on the same pattern instead of trying to read everything at once.
The same C triad can be read as letter names or as roles. Tap either diagram, then flip Names / Degrees on the board below.
Place notes in Chord Analyzer to turn a shape into roles. Pin the root when context demands it, compare inversions, and notice which tones are doubled or omitted.
Compare a root-position Cmaj7 with C/E. Send proposed scales back to Explore and check the chord against the larger collection.
Finish in Drills, where the board stops supplying the answer. Finding a degree, building ii–V–I, and naming an inversion test different kinds of recall.
Use a short cycle: explore a concept, analyze one example, then drill it. Return to Display only to diagnose a miss, and repeat until the location and sound agree.

Ionian.desc: The major scale itself. No real tension to resolve — the sound of home and a happy ending.

Dorian.desc: A minor scale with a bright 6th. Santana solos, Irish folk, and modal jazz — sadness that still smiles.

Phrygian.desc: The ♭2 gives it a distinctly Spanish / Andalusian flavor. Flamenco and heavy-metal riffs live here.

Lydian.desc: The ♯4 makes everything feel airy and unresolved — film scores, dream-pop shimmer, classic Sci-Fi wonder.

Mixolydian.desc: The major scale with a bluesy flattened 7th — the sound of rock, blues, and Irish folk.

Aeolian.desc: The natural minor scale — Western musicТs default for sadness, drama and dark emotion.

Locrian.desc: The tonic triad is diminished, so nothing ever truly resolves — dread, chaos, and deliberate “wrongness”.

Harmonic Minor.desc: The raised 7th over a ♭6 creates a signature leap — klezmer, gypsy, metal and classical minor melodies.

Locrian #6.desc: Locrian with a raised 6th — shadowy and unstable.

Ionian #5.desc: A major scale with a sharpened 5th — chords wobble between major and augmented.

Dorian #4.desc: Dorian with a raised 4th — a jazzy, slightly exotic minor sound.

Altered bb7.desc: An altered dominant scale full of chromatic tension.

Melodic Minor.desc: The jazz minor — a minor scale that rises with a major sound, a favorite for soloing over minor chords.

Dorian b2.desc: Dorian with a flattened 2nd — dark and exotic.

Lydian Augmented.desc: Lydian with a raised 5th — floating, majestic film-score material.

Lydian Dominant.desc: A dominant 7 chord with a ♯11 — the jazz-fusion and bebop dominant sound.

Mixolydian b6.desc: A dominant scale that bends toward minor — melancholic.

Locrian #2.desc: Locrian with a raised 2nd — dark and unstable.

Super Locrian.desc: The altered scale — every note is a tension note, built for playing over altered dominant chords.

Phrygian Dominant.desc: The Andalusian sound of flamenco, gypsy jazz and Middle-Eastern metal — a dominant chord with a flat 2nd.

Harmonic Major.desc: The major scale with a flattened 6th — Ravel and jazz harmony love its dual major/minor colors.

Dorian b5.desc: Dorian with a flattened 5th — a minor sound with a diminished core.

Phrygian b4.desc: Phrygian with a flattened 4th — an unusual, ancient-sounding color.

Lydian b3.desc: Lydian bent toward minor — the tonic wavers between major and minor.

Mixolydian b2.desc: A dominant sound with a Phrygian lean — tense and dramatic.

Lydian Augmented #2.desc: An extreme Lydian variant with three raised notes.

Lydian #2 #6.desc: An exotic Lydian variant with raised 2nd and 6th.

Lydian #5 b7.desc: A dominant Lydian variant with a raised 5th.

Ionian #4 b6.desc: Major with raised 4th and flattened 6th — odd and rare.

Phrygian #2 #4.desc: Phrygian with raised 2nd and 4th — exotic and unstable.

Neapolitan Minor.desc: The Neapolitan minor — a dark classical mode with a flat 2nd.

Phrygian #3.desc: A Phrygian-dominant-like sound — flamenco and Arabic color.

Mixolydian #2.desc: A dominant mode with a sharpened 2nd.

Lydian #2 b6.desc: Lydian bent minor with a raised 2nd — dark and rare.

majorPentatonic.desc: Five notes with no half-steps — almost impossible to sound wrong. Pop, folk, country and blues.

minorPentatonic.desc: The go-to scale for rock and blues guitar solos.

blues.desc: Minor pentatonic with a flattened 5th — the note that bends and wails.

dominant.desc: The Mixolydian sound — a dominant scale for bluesy rock.

wholeTone.desc: No tonal center at all — Debussy and jazz use it for a hazy, unsettled shimmer.

diminished.desc: Alternating whole and half steps — an 8-note scale full of built-in tension.

augmented.desc: Two augmented triads stacked — Debussy and Ravel use it for a hazy, glowing sound.

diminishedHW.desc: The half-whole diminished — the classic dominant-altered scale.

chromatic.desc: All twelve notes — total chromatic color, atonal and free.

messiaen3.desc: MessiaenТs Mode 3 — a symmetrical 9-note scale with a liturgical shimmer.

messiaen5.desc: Messiaen Mode 5 — a sparse 6-note symmetric scale.

messiaen6.desc: Messiaen Mode 6 — two interlocking tritone shapes.

messiaen7.desc: MessiaenТs Mode 7 — an almost-chromatic scale of 10 notes.

suspendedPentatonic.desc: The Egyptian / Yo scale — a pentatonic with a suspended, open sound.

dominantPentatonic.desc: Pentatonic built on the dominant notes — a blues-friendly five-note set.

hirajoshi.desc: A classic koto tuning scale — sparse and evocative.

iwato.desc: A dark Japanese scale with flat 2nd and flat 5th.

insen.desc: Another traditional Japanese scale — sparse and elegant.

pelog.desc: A Javanese/Balinese gamelan scale of seven tones.

marwa.desc: An Arabic maqam scale — dark and dignified.

bluesMajor.desc: The major blues scale — a bright pentatonic with a passing blue note.

hexatonicMajor.desc: A six-note major scale with a wide gap between 5th and 7th.

hexatonicMinor.desc: A six-note minor scale with big expressive leaps.

prometheus.desc: The Scriabin "mystic" chord scale — mystical and brooding.

bebopMinor.desc: Minor with a chromatic passing note between 3rd and 5th.

majorSixDiminished.desc: The Barry Harris major scale — major with a passing chromatic 3rd.

persian.desc: The Persian scale — exotic and regal, used in traditional Persian music.

todi.desc: A Hindustani raga scale — devotional and serious.

purvi.desc: A raga scale built on double-harmonic color.

mixolydianAugmented.desc: A dominant scale with a raised 5th — bright and tense.

lydianMinor.desc: Lydian bent toward minor — airy and unresolved.

hungarianMajor.desc: The Hungarian gypsy major — dark, fiery and folk-inflected.

locrianNatural2.desc: Locrian with a natural 2nd — dissonant but less sharp.
